name: approve
summary: show what a proposed operation will do to a machine, then let it run; several names: one plan and one answer each; without a name, list the operations that wait for approval
description:
The operator never acts on a machine before a person approves the plan.
approve prints the plan first: the machine, its BMC, each step in order, the
media it mounts, the boot target, and for an OS install the node, its address
and the disk that will be overwritten. Then it asks "Approve? [y/N]".
The question waits five minutes. After a yes, approve reads the operation
again and approves it only if it is the same object and its plan reads the
same; otherwise nothing changes and you look at the new plan.

The approval is recorded as your cluster user, and it cannot be changed
afterwards. Whether you can approve an operation that you proposed yourself is
a site setting (selfApproval, default Allowed); where the site forbids it,
another person must approve. The operator's own identity never approves.

Operations live in the operator's namespace, pk-metal. You can give the name
as it appears in pk-metal status (pk-metal/<name>) or use -n.

With several names, approve shows the plan of each in turn and asks about
each one on its own. A no leaves that operation as it is and goes on with the
next. The exit status is 1 if any of them was not approved.

The plan also lists the guards that annotations lift for the operation
(metal.pk.io/override-cluster-guard, metal.pk.io/ignore-window), with the
reason each one gives. Read them before you answer.

Without a terminal (in a script or a pipe), approve does not ask: it refuses
unless you give --yes.
examples: pk-metal approve                                  list what waits for approval
pk-metal approve --yes provision-node1-1a2b3c4d   approve in a script
